messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: packaging plans
parts:
Here's my current thinking about how to package r/stan. Comments welcome.

The first part of the changes involve stuff that is not Debian-specific,
though it may be Unix-specific. I'll make a configure.ac that looks for
the libraries currently used in several places, starting with where they
are now in the tarball. This way they should work fine as things stand
now, but they will allow using libraries and headers that are already on
the system.

It doesn't look as if the current stan system uses configure, and that
many configure like operations (e.g., discovering the type of compiler)
are done in the makefiles. So I wonder a bit if introducing configure
is a good idea, though it seems to me the natural way to approach the
problem of discovering libraries. I'm also not sure how portable this
is to windows.

Then, getting into the Debian specific stuff, I'll strip out the
external headers from the stan and make at least one package that
contains the headers (stan-dev) and depends on other packages that
provide boost and eigen (also g++). stan-dev might contain everything
else (e.g., compiled stanc), or there might be a stan package too. My
interest is in rstan, and it's the stan headers I need for rstan.

The rstan package would similarly start from source with the external
headers, including the stan headers, removed. It too would have a
configure script for finding those headers, and it would depend on those
headers, including stan-dev.

r/stan is a bit unusual. For the generic package foo, the foo package
holds the executable, used by the user at run-time, and foo-dev holds
headers and libraries that a developer who was using the package would
need at compile time. But for stan, run time is compile time, although
different things are compiled for the user (namely their .stan programs)
than for the "adminstrator" (e.g., stanc or the equivalent R library).

I looked a little to see if there is, or could be, a common stan library
used by stan and rstan. That is, could there be a librstan that uses
libstan? rstan/rstan/rstan/src seems to be the only rstan specific C++
code, and the files there are mostly versions of ones found in the stan
tree (after translating names like a_b_c to a/b/c). Some of them are
clearly different: stanc.cpp and chains.cpp have R interfaces. Others
have only an include line that refers to the equivalent stan file. This
suggests that at least in principle rstan could depend on stan
libraries. The simplest path for now is likely for the rstan package to
rely on stan-dev only for headers.

Ross

If you change our basic installation procedure, we want to test it
thoroughly. What we have now is working pretty well for our use
cases, and I don't want to add complications that are going to jam
up our mailing lists with requests for help on installation and
compatibility with external libraries, versions of Boost and Eigen,
etc.

> It doesn't look as if the current stan system uses configure, and that many configure like operations (e.g., discovering

I don't think the makefile does compiler discovery, just
config. But I could be wrong. It does check for platform in
various places.

We didn't want to use configure because I (Bob) could never
get it to work on any of the packages I tried to install, so
I wanted to keep our releases simpler and depend on fewer other
tools. I found Boost and Eigen both trivial to use from source.

I have no idea what the right thing to do for Debian is,
but we should follow standard operating procedure there. It doesn't
need to be compatible down to config with our other Stan distributions.
That is, you can build a debian-specific makefile and configure if
that's the right thing to do.

Not sure what you mean by headers here. Stan leans heavily
on templates, so for the most part, the headers are the source, too.

> too would have a configure script for finding those headers, and it would depend on those headers, including stan-dev.
>
> r/stan is a bit unusual.
Do you mean the same package we're calling "RStan" (package name "rstan" in R)?

> For the generic package foo, the foo package holds the executable, used by the user at
> run-time, and foo-dev holds headers and libraries that a developer who was using the package would need at compile
> time. But for stan, run time is compile time, although different things are compiled for the user (namely their .stan
> programs) than for the "adminstrator" (e.g., stanc or the equivalent R library).
Right.

> I looked a little to see if there is, or could be, a common stan library used by stan and rstan. That is, could there
> be a librstan that uses libstan? rstan/rstan/rstan/src seems to be the only rstan specific C++ code, and the files
> there are mostly versions of ones found in the stan tree (after translating names like a_b_c to a/b/c). Some of them
> are clearly different: stanc.cpp and chains.cpp have R interfaces. Others have only an include line that refers to the
> equivalent stan file. This suggests that at least in principle rstan could depend on stan libraries. The simplest path
> for now is likely for the rstan package to rely on stan-dev only for headers.

Yes, RStan just depends on the Stan libs. It adds some of
its own, too, for the R interfaces.

Just my opinions and I'm probably the least skilled of all of
our developers at config and make, so take them with a grain of salt.

- Bob

Ben

5 will probably require the most work. A Debian package providing an interface to Stan from R would be different in non-trivial ways from the existing rstan R package, although both should have equivalent functionality.

I would think that stanc, print, and any other binaries, could go in a single Debian package "stan". Is there any reason to separate them?
Binaries with overly generic names like print will probably need to become stan-print, or something like that (for Debian).


Ross

The preferred way in debian-land is *not* to put debian stuff in the
"upstream" stan source at all (not even inside a debian/ folder). It
all gets applied downstream. Debian maintainers can then look after
the debian-specific customisations without having to (for example)
have access to the stan repo. If I read right, Ross is going with that
approach - i.e. the main stan repo won't see any changes.

Dan
